## 1. Uso previsto para Fase 4-5 v1

Fuente para Fase 4-5 v1 sobre prediccion de ancho de banda + seleccion de bitrate con DRL. Relevante para explorar modelos que no solo imitan acciones sino que estiman capacidad futura/segura antes de decidir, especialmente si queremos reducir rebuffer por sobreestimacion de throughput.

```text
IEEE TRANSACTIONS ON NETWORK AND SERVICE MANAGEMENT
1
Enhancing Adaptive Video Streaming through
Bandwidth Prediction with Deep Reinforcement
Learning
Xin Hu, Xiantao Jiang, Member, IEEE, F. Richard Yu, Fellow, IEEE, and Victor C.M. Leung, Life Fellow, IEEE
Abstract—With the development of HTTP-based video stream-
ing, Adaptive Bitrate (ABR) algorithms have become crucial for
optimizing video quality. These algorithms dynamically select
the bitrate of video chunks based on factors such as network
throughput and playback buffer occupancy. However, the volatil-
ity of network throughput, conflicting Quality of Experience
(QoE) objectives, and cascading effects in decision-making pose
significant challenges for ABR algorithms to accurately determine
bitrate selections, leading to substantial revenue losses for content
providers. This paper proposes a bandwidth prediction-based
ABR algorithm for video streaming, termed the BPA algorithm,
which consists of two components: a Bandwidth Prediction Model
(BPM) and a Bitrate Selection Model (BSM). The BPM leverages
a Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (BiLSTM) network
for bandwidth prediction, while the BSM adopts an Actor-Critic
reinforcement learning framework. A reward function based
on bandwidth prediction accuracy is proposed, and an end-
to-end joint optimization loss function is designed to train the
model for optimal video bitrate selection. Under various network
conditions, the BPA algorithm outperforms existing baseline
algorithms, achieving an improvement of nearly 31.9% compared
to traditional heuristic methods and a 9% enhancement over
other deep reinforcement learning-based approaches. The BPA
algorithm demonstrates excellent performance in terms of bitrate
smoothness and QoE.
Index Terms—Adaptive Bitrate (ABR), deep reinforcement
learning (DRL), quality of experience (QoE), bandwidth predic-
tion, Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (BiLSTM).

As traditional media transitions to the Internet, video content
providers face the challenge of delivering an exceptional
quality of user experience (QoE) [4], [5]. Traditional quality of
service (QoS) focuses on platform-centric optimization, where
resources are allocated primarily to platform construction and
maintenance [6], often at the expense of user experience qual-
ity, sometimes even resulting in inefficient resource use. Con-
sequently, increasing attention is being directed toward QoE,
which adopts a user-centered approach, aiming to improve
user satisfaction by effectively capturing users’ subjective
experience throughout their interaction. In video streaming,
QoE represents the core competitiveness of the industry. A
high QoE serves as a critical factor in retaining subscribers,
boosting revenue for video providers, and is key to their
competitive success.
Studies have shown that when videos suffer from issues
such as low quality, slow startup, or laggy playback, users are
unlikely to watch the entire video, posing significant risks for
video content providers [7], [8]. Currently, major platforms
such as YouTube, Netflix, Facebook, and TikTok employ
Adaptive Bitrate (ABR) algorithms to deliver video services,
with the goal of enhancing user experience quality. Prominent
ABR implementations include Apple’s HTTP Live Streaming
(HLS) [9], Microsoft’s Live Smooth Streaming (Smooth) [10],
and Adobe’s Adaptive Streaming (HDS) [11]. To address
variations across providers, the Moving Picture Experts Group
(MPEG) standardized such protocols under Dynamic Adaptive
Streaming over HTTP (DASH) in 2014 [12].
DASH is currently the primary method for online video
delivery, as illustrated in Fig. 1. In a DASH system, lossy video
sequences are generated from the original video at various
bitrate levels, with higher bitrates providing better quality.
These sequences are segmented based on a fixed time length.
The original video is ultimately divided into different bitrate
segments and stored in uniform sizes on an HTTP server.
```

### 8.1. modelo algoritmo arquitectura

Palabras clave usadas: `model, algorithm, architecture, framework, policy, neural, network, deep reinforcement, reinforcement learning, DRL, DQN, PPO, A2C, A3C, actor, critic, agent, meta, meta-learning, MAML, offline reinforcement, curriculum, VAE, variational autoencoder, LSTM, BiLSTM, GRU, CNN, predictor, bandwidth prediction, Plume, Gelato, Ahaggar, CausalSim, IMDP, domain-specific prior`

**Fragmento 1 - p. 1 - score 11:**

This paper proposes a bandwidth prediction-based ABR algorithm for video streaming, termed the BPA algorithm, which consists of two components: a Bandwidth Prediction Model (BPM) and a Bitrate Selection Model (BSM). The BPM leverages a Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (BiLSTM) network for bandwidth prediction, while the BSM adopts an Actor-Critic reinforcement learning framework. A reward function based on bandwidth prediction accuracy is proposed, and an end- to-end joint optimization loss function is designed to train the model for optimal video bitrate selection. Under various network conditions, the BPA algorithm outperforms existing baseline algorithms, achieving an improvement of nearly 31.9% compared to traditional heuristic methods and a 9% enhancement over other deep reinforcement learning-based approaches.

**Fragmento 2 - p. 2 - score 10:**

This solution incorporates two modules to tackle the bitrate selection problem: the Bandwidth Prediction Model (BPM) and the Bitrate Selection Model (BSM). Specifically, BPM employs a bidirectional long short-term memory neu- ral network (BiLSTM) [13] for bandwidth prediction, with deep learning models yielding improved prediction accuracy compared to traditional methods. In the case of BSM, an actor-critic framework in deep reinforcement learning is used, where the actor outputs bitrate actions and the critic outputs state values [14]. Furthermore, bandwidth prediction accuracy is integrated into the reward function, and the model is trained via a novel end-to-end joint loss function.

**Fragmento 5 - p. 4 - score 9:**

This paper proposes a bandwidth prediction-based ABR algorithm for video streaming, termed the BPA algorithm, which consists of two components: a Bandwidth Prediction Model (BPM) and a Bitrate Selection Model (BSM). The BPM leverages a Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (BiLSTM) network for bandwidth prediction, while the BSM adopts an Actor-Critic reinforcement learning framework. A reward function based on bandwidth prediction accuracy is proposed, and an end- to-end joint optimization loss function is designed to train the model for optimal video bitrate selection. Under various network conditions, the BPA algorithm outperforms existing baseline algorithms, achieving an improvement of nearly 31.9% compared to traditional heuristic methods and a 9% enhancement over other deep reinforcement learning-based approaches.

Third, current DRL reward designs typically focus solely on QoE metrics, overlooking the role of prediction accuracy in improving long-term streaming stability. Without incorporating prediction error as part of the optimization ob- jective, the learned policies may lack robustness in fluctuating environments. This paper proposes a novel solution to address the issue of inaccurate bandwidth prediction in ABR algorithms. In the current era of 4G and 5G, network bandwidth is increasing, but even minor network fluctuations can cause video streaming lag, making accurate bandwidth prediction crucial for enhanc- ing QoE.

However, the volatil- ity of network throughput, conflicting Quality of Experience (QoE) objectives, and cascading effects in decision-making pose significant challenges for ABR algorithms to accurately determine bitrate selections, leading to substantial revenue losses for content providers.

Seamless transitions between bitrates ensure imperceptible quality adjustments during playback. B. Adaptive Bitrate Algorithm The ABR algorithm is an effective method for dynamically adjusting the quality of streaming video to enhance the user experience. Currently, ABR algorithms are broadly categorized into two main types: traditional heuristic algorithms and machine learning-based algorithms [16]. Key traditional heuristic algorithms include the follow- ing: Buffer Occupancy-based Lyapunov Algorithm (BOLA) [17], which employs Lyapunov optimization to manage buffer occupancy and reduce rebuffering time by adjusting buffer capacity; Sun et al. [18], who utilized a Markov model to predict network bandwidth availability, enabling more accurate bitrate selection; and the Festive algorithm [19], which esti- mates bitrate using a harmonic mean based on recent network throughput data.

**Fragmento 5 - p. 3 - score 6:**

Clients initiate segmented requests based on parsed MPD data, enabling dy- namic balance between network bandwidth and video quality. Specifically, the original video is encoded at varying bitrates or resolutions on the server, then split into short-duration chunks to form corresponding media segment files. An MPD file is subsequently created, containing metadata such as basic information about the video segments, serving as a “playback guide” for clients. Clients first retrieve the MPD file, then dynamically select appropriate bitrate segments for download by real-time monitoring of network bandwidth and local cache status. Playback commences once a sufficient number of segments are cached, with subsequent segments downloaded asynchronously.

The two objectives appear separable in their abstract form, they are implicitly coupled through the state representation and policy decision process. The predicted bandwidth influences bitrate selection, which in turn determines QoE. Therefore, independent optimization may lead to suboptimal coordination between prediction and decision-making modules. We adopt the Simple Additive Weighting (SAW) method to transform the multi-objective problem into a single-objective formulation.

Despite the progress made by existing ABR algorithms, several key limitations remain that directly motivate our pro- posed system design. First, many traditional ABR methods, rely on heuristic or fixed-rule bandwidth estimators. These techniques often struggle to adapt to the dynamic and volatile nature of modern mobile and wireless networks, leading to inaccurate bandwidth predictions and unstable bitrate deci- sions. Second, while some deep reinforcement learning-based ABR algorithms, have demonstrated improved QoE, they often treat bandwidth prediction and bitrate selection as separate problems. This disjointed modeling can result in suboptimal decision-making, where the bitrate chosen by the agent does not fully reflect the actual network conditions.

This paper proposes a bandwidth prediction-based ABR algorithm for video streaming, termed the BPA algorithm, which consists of two components: a Bandwidth Prediction Model (BPM) and a Bitrate Selection Model (BSM). The BPM leverages a Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (BiLSTM) network for bandwidth prediction, while the BSM adopts an Actor-Critic reinforcement learning framework. A reward function based on bandwidth prediction accuracy is proposed, and an end- to-end joint optimization loss function is designed to train the model for optimal video bitrate selection. Under various network conditions, the BPA algorithm outperforms existing baseline algorithms, achieving an improvement of nearly 31.9% compared to traditional heuristic methods and a 9% enhancement over other deep reinforcement learning-based approaches.

MPC (Model Predictive Control) algorithm selects bitrates by solving a QoE maximization problem across several future video segments. By directly optimizing for QoE objectives, MPC often outperforms methods that rely on fixed rules. How- ever, our experiments reveal that MPC’s performance hinges on the accuracy of the system dynamics model, particularly in predicting future network throughput. The MPC algorithm makes predictions by incorporating throughput as an input to the dynamic system model, but this dependency introduces prediction errors. When these predictions deviate significantly, the resulting ABR decisions can be suboptimal. Conversely, the Pensieve algorithm leverages deep rein- forcement learning to identify optimal policies more precisely, allowing multiple agents to interact with distinct states simul- taneously.

**Fragmento 21 - p. 4 - score 2:**

Several reinforcement learning-based approaches have demonstrated this potential. Claeys et al. [22] applied Q-learning in ABR, where the algorithm learns and stores state value functions in a tabular format rather than relying on neural networks. Mao et al. [23] introduced a Reinforcement Learning-based ABR (ABRL) algorithm that optimizes QoE through a Bayesian-enhanced [24] linear policy to reduce latency. However, the limitations of linear functions in fully capturing ABR dynamics can compromise the performance. Pensieve [15] marked the beginning of deep reinforcement learning for ABR, employing an asynchronous dominance approach [14] to train a neural network to predict optimal ABR strategies, where the agent continuously learns through interaction with system states.

**Fragmento 22 - p. 4 - score 2:**

Article [28] proposed a quality-aware adaptive video streaming system based on imitation learning named Comyco. Comyco trains its policy by imitating expert trajec- tories, significantly enhancing sample efficiency and training speed, and demonstrating outstanding performance in video quality perception.

**Fragmento 13 - p. 1 - score 3:**

This paper proposes a bandwidth prediction-based ABR algorithm for video streaming, termed the BPA algorithm, which consists of two components: a Bandwidth Prediction Model (BPM) and a Bitrate Selection Model (BSM). The BPM leverages a Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (BiLSTM) network for bandwidth prediction, while the BSM adopts an Actor-Critic reinforcement learning framework. A reward function based on bandwidth prediction accuracy is proposed, and an end- to-end joint optimization loss function is designed to train the model for optimal video bitrate selection. Under various network conditions, the BPA algorithm outperforms existing baseline algorithms, achieving an improvement of nearly 31.9% compared to traditional heuristic methods and a 9% enhancement over other deep reinforcement learning-based approaches.

The prediction error loss is in- corporated into the model, and a new reward function is constructed by combining QoE, which takes prediction error into account.

Studies have shown that when videos suffer from issues such as low quality, slow startup, or laggy playback, users are unlikely to watch the entire video, posing significant risks for video content providers [7], [8]. Currently, major platforms such as YouTube, Netflix, Facebook, and TikTok employ Adaptive Bitrate (ABR) algorithms to deliver video services, with the goal of enhancing user experience quality. Prominent ABR implementations include Apple’s HTTP Live Streaming (HLS) [9], Microsoft’s Live Smooth Streaming (Smooth) [10], and Adobe’s Adaptive Streaming (HDS) [11]. To address variations across providers, the Moving Picture Experts Group (MPEG) standardized such protocols under Dynamic Adaptive Streaming over HTTP (DASH) in 2014 [12].

MPC (Model Predictive Control) algorithm selects bitrates by solving a QoE maximization problem across several future video segments. By directly optimizing for QoE objectives, MPC often outperforms methods that rely on fixed rules. How- ever, our experiments reveal that MPC’s performance hinges on the accuracy of the system dynamics model, particularly in predicting future network throughput. The MPC algorithm makes predictions by incorporating throughput as an input to the dynamic system model, but this dependency introduces prediction errors. When these predictions deviate significantly, the resulting ABR decisions can be suboptimal. Conversely, the Pensieve algorithm leverages deep rein- forcement learning to identify optimal policies more precisely, allowing multiple agents to interact with distinct states simul- taneously.

This paper proposes a bandwidth prediction-based ABR algorithm for video streaming, termed the BPA algorithm, which consists of two components: a Bandwidth Prediction Model (BPM) and a Bitrate Selection Model (BSM). The BPM leverages a Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (BiLSTM) network for bandwidth prediction, while the BSM adopts an Actor-Critic reinforcement learning framework. A reward function based on bandwidth prediction accuracy is proposed, and an end- to-end joint optimization loss function is designed to train the model for optimal video bitrate selection. Under various network conditions, the BPA algorithm outperforms existing baseline algorithms, achieving an improvement of nearly 31.9% compared to traditional heuristic methods and a 9% enhancement over other deep reinforcement learning-based approaches.

MPC (Model Predictive Control) algorithm selects bitrates by solving a QoE maximization problem across several future video segments. By directly optimizing for QoE objectives, MPC often outperforms methods that rely on fixed rules. How- ever, our experiments reveal that MPC’s performance hinges on the accuracy of the system dynamics model, particularly in predicting future network throughput. The MPC algorithm makes predictions by incorporating throughput as an input to the dynamic system model, but this dependency introduces prediction errors. When these predictions deviate significantly, the resulting ABR decisions can be suboptimal. Conversely, the Pensieve algorithm leverages deep rein- forcement learning to identify optimal policies more precisely, allowing multiple agents to interact with distinct states simul- taneously.

**Fragmento 10 - p. 1 - score 2:**

This paper proposes a bandwidth prediction-based ABR algorithm for video streaming, termed the BPA algorithm, which consists of two components: a Bandwidth Prediction Model (BPM) and a Bitrate Selection Model (BSM). The BPM leverages a Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (BiLSTM) network for bandwidth prediction, while the BSM adopts an Actor-Critic reinforcement learning framework. A reward function based on bandwidth prediction accuracy is proposed, and an end- to-end joint optimization loss function is designed to train the model for optimal video bitrate selection. Under various network conditions, the BPA algorithm outperforms existing baseline algorithms, achieving an improvement of nearly 31.9% compared to traditional heuristic methods and a 9% enhancement over other deep reinforcement learning-based approaches.

Studies have shown that when videos suffer from issues such as low quality, slow startup, or laggy playback, users are unlikely to watch the entire video, posing significant risks for video content providers [7], [8]. Currently, major platforms such as YouTube, Netflix, Facebook, and TikTok employ Adaptive Bitrate (ABR) algorithms to deliver video services, with the goal of enhancing user experience quality. Prominent ABR implementations include Apple’s HTTP Live Streaming (HLS) [9], Microsoft’s Live Smooth Streaming (Smooth) [10], and Adobe’s Adaptive Streaming (HDS) [11]. Enhancing Adaptive Video Streaming through
```text
Bandwidth Prediction with Deep Reinforcement
Learning
Xin Hu, Xiantao Jiang, Member, IEEE, F. Richard Yu, Fellow, IEEE, and Victor C.M. Leung, Life Fellow, IEEE
Abstract—With the development of HTTP-based video stream-
ing, Adaptive Bitrate (ABR) algorithms have become crucial for
optimizing video quality. These algorithms dynamically select
the bitrate of video chunks based on factors such as network
throughput and playback buffer occupancy. However, the volatil-
ity of network throughput, conflicting Quality of Experience
(QoE) objectives, and cascading effects in decision-making pose
significant challenges for ABR algorithms to accurately determine
bitrate selections, leading to substantial revenue losses for content
providers. This paper proposes a bandwidth prediction-based
ABR algorithm for video streaming, termed the BPA algorithm,
which consists of two components: a Bandwidth Prediction Model
(BPM) and a Bitrate Selection Model (BSM). The BPM leverages
a Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (BiLSTM) network
for bandwidth prediction, while the BSM adopts an Actor-Critic
reinforcement learning framework. A reward function based
on bandwidth prediction accuracy is proposed, and an end-
to-end joint optimization loss function is designed to train the
model for optimal video bitrate selection. Under various network
conditions, the BPA algorithm outperforms existing baseline
algorithms, achieving an improvement of nearly 31.9% compared
to traditional heuristic methods and a 9% enhancement over
other deep reinforcement learning-based approaches. The BPA
algorithm demonstrates excellent performance in terms of bitrate
smoothness and QoE.
Index Terms—Adaptive Bitrate (ABR), deep reinforcement
learning (DRL), quality of experience (QoE), bandwidth predic-
tion, Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (BiLSTM).
```

```text
Despite the progress made by existing ABR algorithms,
several key limitations remain that directly motivate our pro-
posed system design. First, many traditional ABR methods,
rely on heuristic or fixed-rule bandwidth estimators. These
techniques often struggle to adapt to the dynamic and volatile
nature of modern mobile and wireless networks, leading to
inaccurate bandwidth predictions and unstable bitrate deci-
sions. Second, while some deep reinforcement learning-based
ABR algorithms, have demonstrated improved QoE, they often
treat bandwidth prediction and bitrate selection as separate
problems. This disjointed modeling can result in suboptimal
decision-making, where the bitrate chosen by the agent does
not fully reflect the actual network conditions. Additionally,
these approaches require large-scale parallel training with
many agents (e.g., 16 or more), leading to significant com-
putational overhead that hampers real-time deployment and
scalability. Third, current DRL reward designs typically focus
solely on QoE metrics, overlooking the role of prediction
accuracy in improving long-term streaming stability. Without
incorporating prediction error as part of the optimization ob-
jective, the learned policies may lack robustness in fluctuating
environments.
This paper proposes a novel solution to address the issue
of inaccurate bandwidth prediction in ABR algorithms. In the
current era of 4G and 5G, network bandwidth is increasing,
but even minor network fluctuations can cause video streaming
lag, making accurate bandwidth prediction crucial for enhanc-
ing QoE. This solution incorporates two modules to tackle
the bitrate selection problem: the Bandwidth Prediction Model
(BPM) and the Bitrate Selection Model (BSM). Specifically,
BPM employs a bidirectional long short-term memory neu-
ral network (BiLSTM) [13] for bandwidth prediction, with
deep learning models yielding improved prediction accuracy
compared to traditional methods. In the case of BSM, an
actor-critic framework in deep reinforcement learning is used,
where the actor outputs bitrate actions and the critic outputs
state values [14]. Furthermore, bandwidth prediction accuracy
is integrated into the reward function, and the model is
trained via a novel end-to-end joint loss function. The main
contributions of this paper are:
1) A new framework is proposed to address the video
streaming ABR problem by jointly training two distinct
models. Additionally, to address the issue of inaccurate
prediction, bandwidth prediction is performed using
BiLSTM, which leverages BiLSTM’s capability to cap-
ture temporal and contextual information in the data,
significantly improving prediction accuracy compared to
previous heuristic methods.
2) To improve prediction accuracy, a novel reward func-
tion and loss function based on bandwidth prediction
precision are introduced. The prediction error loss is in-
corporated into the model, and a new reward function is
constructed by combining QoE, which takes prediction
error into account. Furthermore, to enhance prediction
accuracy, an end-to-end joint optimization loss function
is proposed. In our experiments, this approach yields
highly desirable results for the model.
3) Utilizing fewer agents and a reduced number of itera-
tions. In deep reinforcement learning, parallel training
with multiple agents and states is considered to allow
agents to interact with different states, thus achieving
better results. In Pensieve [15] algorithms, 8-16 agents
are typically required, with more agents yielding better
results but significantly increasing computation time. For
our model, however, using only two agents achieves
results comparable to the baseline algorithm, with sig-
nificantly fewer than 100,000 iteration rounds.

II. BACKGROUND AND RELATED WORK
A. DASH Overview
DASH, standardized by MPEG, stands as a prevailing
adaptive streaming technology. It operates independently of
proprietary transmission protocols, leveraging HTTP/HTTPS
for data delivery while maintaining compatibility with ex-
isting network architectures (including CDNs, servers, and
browsers). This technology finds extensive application across
video streaming platforms, live broadcasting, and OTT (Over-
the-Top) services.
As illustrated in Fig. 1, the DASH system comprises three
core components: a media presentation server, an HTTP server,
and clients. On the server side, encoding tools (such as
FFmpeg) are utilized to generate multi-bitrate video segments
and produce an MPD (Media Presentation Description) file
```

```text
Specifically, the original video is encoded at varying bitrates
or resolutions on the server, then split into short-duration

status. Playback commences once a sufficient number of

asynchronously. Seamless transitions between bitrates ensure

B. Adaptive Bitrate Algorithm
The ABR algorithm is an effective method for dynamically
adjusting the quality of streaming video to enhance the user
experience. Currently, ABR algorithms are broadly categorized
into two main types: traditional heuristic algorithms and
machine learning-based algorithms [16].
Key traditional heuristic algorithms include the follow-
ing: Buffer Occupancy-based Lyapunov Algorithm (BOLA)
[17], which employs Lyapunov optimization to manage buffer
occupancy and reduce rebuffering time by adjusting buffer
capacity; Sun et al. [18], who utilized a Markov model to
predict network bandwidth availability, enabling more accurate
bitrate selection; and the Festive algorithm [19], which esti-
mates bitrate using a harmonic mean based on recent network
throughput data. Additionally, Huang et al. [20] introduced a
```

```text
IEEE TRANSACTIONS ON NETWORK AND SERVICE MANAGEMENT
4
segmented function model to map the relationship between
playback buffer size and video block bitrate, facilitating better
bitrate control. Yin et al. [21] applied Model Predictive Control
(MPC), a cybernetic approach that combines buffer occupancy
with network throughput, to predict optimal video bitrate
dynamically.
Machine learning-based approaches for ABR can be broadly
divided into reinforcement learning and deep reinforcement
learning techniques. Unlike traditional heuristic algorithms,
which rely on fixed control rules such as estimated net-
work throughput (“rate-based” methods), playback buffer size
(“buffer-based” schemes), or a combination of both, these
machine learning methods do not require predefined con-
trol rules, offering the potential for higher QoE in video
streaming. Several reinforcement learning-based approaches
have demonstrated this potential. Claeys et al. [22] applied
Q-learning in ABR, where the algorithm learns and stores
state value functions in a tabular format rather than relying on
neural networks. Mao et al. [23] introduced a Reinforcement
Learning-based ABR (ABRL) algorithm that optimizes QoE
through a Bayesian-enhanced [24] linear policy to reduce
latency. However, the limitations of linear functions in fully
capturing ABR dynamics can compromise the performance.
Pensieve [15] marked the beginning of deep reinforcement
learning for ABR, employing an asynchronous dominance
approach [14] to train a neural network to predict optimal
ABR strategies, where the agent continuously learns through
interaction with system states. Expanding on deep learning
techniques, Lekharu et al. [25] utilized a Long Short-Term
Memory (LSTM) neural network [26] to capture temporal
patterns in streaming data, leading to improved QoE. Huo et al.
[27] introduced a meta-learning approach that combines multi-
task deep reinforcement learning with meta-learning, resulting
in the Meta-learning Framework for Multi-user Preferences
(MLMP), which customizes QoE optimization for diverse user
preferences. Article [28] proposed a quality-aware adaptive
video streaming system based on imitation learning named
Comyco. Comyco trains its policy by imitating expert trajec-
tories, significantly enhancing sample efficiency and training
speed, and demonstrating outstanding performance in video
quality perception. Huang et al. [29] proposed a buffer-aware
ABR algorithm that jointly manages bitrate selection and
maximum buffer capacity, effectively minimizing data wastage
by controlling buffer overflow. Recently, Huang et al. [30] pre-
sented Jade, an adaptive video stream optimization system that
leverages human feedback reinforcement learning. It combines
linear models and deep neural network (DNN) architectures
and introduces smooth training and online trajectory selection
mechanisms to achieve superior QoE performance.
The ABR algorithm bases its bitrate decisions on real-
time observations of factors like network throughput and
buffer usage, aiming to maximize user QoE by dynamically
selecting optimal bitrates. However, ABR systems face several
challenges in adapting to network and user dynamics:
• Network Complexity: Real-world networks are complex
and highly variable, making accurate prediction challeng-
ing.
• Conflicting QoE Objectives: Balancing metrics such as
high video quality, low startup latency, and minimal
playback interruptions often results in trade-offs.
• Cascading Decision Impacts: Decisions in ABR algo-
rithms can have cascading effects. For instance, selecting
a high bitrate may drain the buffer and lead to playback
interruptions, while underutilizing bandwidth can degrade
video quality, potentially causing users to leave early and
resulting in data waste.
MPC (Model Predictive Control) algorithm selects bitrates
by solving a QoE maximization problem across several future
video segments. By directly optimizing for QoE objectives,
MPC often outperforms methods that rely on fixed rules. How-
ever, our experiments reveal that MPC’s performance hinges
on the accuracy of the system dynamics model, particularly
in predicting future network throughput. The MPC algorithm
makes predictions by incorporating throughput as an input to
the dynamic system model, but this dependency introduces
prediction errors. When these predictions deviate significantly,
the resulting ABR decisions can be suboptimal.
Conversely, the Pensieve algorithm leverages deep rein-
forcement learning to identify optimal policies more precisely,
allowing multiple agents to interact with distinct states simul-
taneously. Despite this, our experiments show that training
Pensieve with multiple agents is computationally intensive,
requiring hundreds of thousands of iterations to converge on
an optimal policy. Additionally, in some scenarios, Pensieve
does not perform as well as MPC in practice. The primary
reason is that Pensieve’s approach to bandwidth utilization
is conservative, prioritizing smoother playback. Consequently,
Pensieve often avoids selecting higher bitrates even when
network bandwidth could support it, potentially diminishing
the viewing experience.
Based on these findings, BPA (Bandwidth Prediction-ABR)
algorithm is proposed to enhance ABR decision-making. The
BPA algorithm aims to improve bitrate selection by accurately
predicting future bandwidth while factoring in bandwidth
forecasts, buffer status, and bitrate information to achieve
precise control over bitrate adjustments.
III. PROPOSED METHOD
To address the issues identified, a new bitrate adaptation
algorithm is proposed, BPA, whose structure is illustrated in
Fig. 2. BPA consists of two main components: the Bandwidth
Prediction Module (BPM) and the Bitrate Selection Module
(BSM), both implemented using neural network architectures.
The detailed working principles of each component are de-
scribed below.
In the context of ABR streaming, the term “bandwidth” is
commonly used to denote the short-term achievable data rate
experienced by the client. In this paper, “bandwidth” refers to
the predicted short-term achievable throughput rather than the
physical link capacity. For clarity, the terms bandwidth and
throughput are used interchangeably throughout this paper to
represent the application-layer achievable data rate observed
from network traces.
```

```text
A. Bandwidth Predict Model
For complex and changing network environments, it is
difficult for ordinary network bandwidth estimation methods
to achieve high prediction accuracy. Thus, in the fast devel-
opment of neural networks, a bandwidth prediction algorithm
based on BiLSTM networks is proposed. Fig. 3 shows the
structure of BPM. The green solid arrows in the figure indicate
forward LSTM and the blue dashed arrows indicate reverse
LSTM. The figure contains three processing sequence, each
containing a BiLSTM network and a regularization layer. As
time T varies, for the received bandwidth data, it first goes
through these three processing sequence and then a linear layer
outputs the result.
BiLSTM is an improved RNN (Recurrent Neural Net-
work) [31]. Specifically designed for processing sequence
data. BiLSTM is able to capture bidirectional dependencies
in a sequence by combining the output of both forward and
backward LSTM networks.
To understand the BiLSTM networks, it is important to
recognize the LSTM networks. LSTMs are a special type
of RNN that is capable of learning long-term dependencies.
LSTM overcomes the problem of gradient vanishing and
gradient explosion in traditional RNNs when dealing with long
sequences by introducing gate mechanisms (input gate, forget
gate, and output gate). BiLSTM improves on it, BiLSTM
runs two independent LSTMs at each time step, one from the
beginning to the end of the sequence (forward LSTM) and the
other from the end to the beginning of the sequence (backward
LSTM). The outputs of these two LSTMs are combined to
be able to consider both forward and backward information.
Compared to traditional LSTMs, BiLSTM is able to take into
account both pre-contextual and post-contextual information
of the sequence [32], which is very beneficial for tasks that
require knowledge of the global context.
In forward LSTM, the first step is to decide what informa-
tion to discard from the cell state C. This decision is completed
through a layer called the forget gate. Here the cell state C
is a vector in the LSTM that allows the network to maintain
and transmit information over long sequences of time. Forget
gate ft was updated to:
```

```text
B. Bitrate Select Model
During the experiments, it was found to be a challenge to
combine the bandwidth prediction model with the bitrate se-
lection model. To deal with this challenge, deep reinforcement
learning algorithms are considered. The predicted bandwidth
value is used as the state value of the reinforcement learning
model so that the bandwidth prediction result and the bit rate
selection are linked. The network model is shown below. BSM
contains three parts, state, actor network, and critic network. It
is important to consider various factors including buffer size,
throughput of past blocks, and bandwidth prediction value in
state. Passing the state value to the actor network gives a bitrate
action, the critic network estimates the next state value based
on the action and finds an optimal action by comparing the
value of the state. The goal is to maximize the cumulative
expected reward. The reasons for selecting the Actor-Critic
network are shown in the appendix.
```

```text
To enhance the synergy between the BPM and
BSM, we further design an end-to-end joint training
mechanism. This enables the gradients during the
reinforcement learning process to not only update
the parameters of the Actor-Critic network but also
backpropagate to the BiLSTM model, thereby im-
proving the consistency between prediction accu-
racy and decision-making quality. To achieve the
unified optimization of QoE maximization and pre-
diction error minimization, we propose a novel loss
function, defined as follows:
L = LDCP P O + λLt(G)
(20)
Among them, λ denotes the influence factor that
regulates the contribution of the prediction task to
the total loss, and Lt(G) is determined by Eq. (8).
3) Using the gradient descent method to update the
parameters, the Actor network parameters θ are
updated as:
θ ←θold + ∇θL + β∇θHθ(St)
(21)
In reinforcement learning, especially in policy-based
methods such as Actor-Critic, the inclusion of en-
tropy regularization terms Hθ(St) in the policy net-
work is an effective way to encourage exploration.
Entropy measures the randomness or uncertainty
of a policy, and increasing the policy entropy can
motivate the agent to explore states that are less
frequently visited under the current policy, thus
avoiding premature convergence to a locally optimal
solution. The β denoted entropy weights here are
used to control the influence of the entropy term,
i.e., the degree of exploration. Increasing values of
β give more weight to the entropy term, encouraging
more exploratory behavior.
• Update of critic network parameter θv
The critic network parameters θv are updated using the
following formula:
θv ←θvold −α∇θv[rt + ϑVθv(St+1) −Vθv(St)]2 (22)
Where α is the importance coefficient controlling the
error of the critic network value function.
• Parallel training
During training, the Actor and Critic networks maintain
shared parameters across parallel agents. A central param-
eter server is employed to aggregate gradients, update the
shared parameters, and distribute the updated weights to
all parallel training instances. Each parallel agent interacts
with an independent environment instance and collects
experience trajectories autonomously. Based on its local
experiences, each agent computes gradients of the joint
loss and periodically pushes them to the central parameter
server for synchronized updates.
In our implementation, two parallel agents are adopted
to
enable
concurrent
training
while
maintaining
a
lightweight architecture. It is worth noting that the central
component functions solely as a parameter synchroniza-
tion mechanism rather than an additional decision-making
agent. More details about parallel training can be found
in the appendix.
IV. EXPERIMENT AND DISCUSSION
In this task, training two models simultaneously presents
a significant challenge. Concurrent training not only increases
the time cost substantially but also makes it difficult to evaluate
the strengths and weaknesses of each model independently.
Therefore, our approach is to first train the BPM on a large-
scale network traces dataset to fine-tune its parameters. Once
the BPM is optimized, then train both the BPM and the BSM
together on a smaller-scale network traces dataset to develop
the optimal ABR algorithm.
A. BPM Training Process
Accurately predicting bandwidth values is a critical chal-
lenge in training the BPM. Many existing ABR algorithms,
such as Pensieve, rely on limited bandwidth traces from a
single dataset, making it difficult to assess model overfitting
and generalization. Furthermore, most large-scale network
measurement datasets are not publicly accessible, and the
available public datasets often lack sufficient scale to ensure
robustness.
To address this limitation, we adopt a large-scale Internet
traffic dataset provided by the UK academic network backbone
[33]. The dataset records total traffic volume (in bits) at fixed
5-minute intervals, resulting in 19,888 records. Since the raw
data represent traffic volume rather than data rate, we convert
the traffic into throughput (Mbps) using
Gt =
Traffict
300 seconds,
thereby obtaining a continuous throughput time series. This
converted throughput sequence is used for pretraining the
BPM. It is important to note that this dataset is employed
solely for predictor pretraining and is not directly used in
ABR environment simulation. Although the backbone traffic
dataset differs in temporal granularity and aggregation level
from per-user throughput traces, it provides diverse long-term
fluctuation patterns that help improve predictor robustness.
BPM Structure: In this paper, due to the limited number
of features in the network traces dataset and to mitigate
model overfitting, a multi-layer processing sequence needs to
be employed. Each sequence includes a BiLSTM layer with
128 neurons and a dropout layer with a dropout rate of 0.1.
Specifically, the data first passes through an initial sequence
where the BiLSTM layer has 128 neurons, followed by a
dropout layer set to 0.1 to prevent overfitting. This means that
10% of neurons are randomly deactivated during each pass,
enhancing the model’s robustness. After processing through
the first sequence, the data continues through a second se-
quence with the same configuration. In total, three processing
sequences are used, after which the data is passed through a
fully connected layer with a single output feature to produce
the final prediction.

necessary to predict the next n data values based on the
```

```text
LSTM models that have the same network structure and

observing the experimental results in Fig. 8 and Fig. 5, it
is found that the LSTM model predicts the last 300 data
extremely poorly compared to the BiLSTM model. Although
LSTM is able to capture some bandwidth trends, it is not
as effective as BiLSTM in handling some peaks. The main
reason is that LSTM is not able to capture the contextual
information of the features in the dataset with a small number
of features as BiLSTM, which leads to inaccurate prediction
results. BiLSTM, due to its bidirectional network structure, is
able to consider both past and future information, so it can still
capture long time contextual information in a small number
of features, and the prediction results are the best.
To further verify the superiority of BiLSTM over LSTM,
we conducted a quantitative comparison on the same dataset,

thereby achieving more accurate bandwidth prediction.
B. BSM Training Process
In the above experiment, the optimal network structure and
parameters for BPM have been determined. In the following,
the BSM needs to train to find an optimal ABR algorithm.
First of all, the dataset needs to be introduced.
Video dataset: The video dataset used for the experiments
is the “Envivio-Dash3” video from the DASH-246 JavaScript
reference client [34] and is encoded at 6 bitrate levels of
{0.3, 0.75, 1.2, 1.85, 2.85, 4.3}Mbps using H.264/MPEG-4 as
codec. The video was divided into 48 chunks with a total
length of 193 seconds. Thus, each block represents about 4
seconds of video playback. Mahimahi was used to simulate
the network conditions of the web tracking corpus [19].
Network traces dataset: The ABR environment simulation
is conducted using publicly available network throughput
traces, including FCC [35], HSDPA [36], and Oboe [37].
These datasets contain timestamped throughput measurements
collected from users watching videos in mobile scenarios such
as trains, cars, and buses. The logs include approximately one
million throughput samples, with each trace lasting about 2000
seconds and recorded at a granularity of 5 seconds. In this
experiment, 300 network traces are randomly selected. Specific
details regarding the dataset are described in the appendix.
BSM Structure: The Actor-Critic reinforcement learning
framework is adopted, where the Actor serves as the policy
```

### Pagina 11

```text
IEEE TRANSACTIONS ON NETWORK AND SERVICE MANAGEMENT
11
network and outputs the corresponding bitrate, while the Critic
acts as the value network, evaluating the policy by assessing
the actions chosen by the Actor under policy π. When the
Actor selects an action a, the Critic provides feedback: if the
action is beneficial, the probability of following that strategy
increases; if not, it decreases.
In detail, the Actor network consists of three one-
dimensional convolutional layers (Conv-1D) with 128 features
and a kernel size of 1, which extract features from throughput,
download time, and block size. Other metrics are processed
through four fully connected (FC) layers, each with 128
neurons. To generate the bitrate action, another FC layer
with 128 neurons is used to downsample the shared network
output. The output from this layer is passed to a final layer,
which applies a softmax function to compute probabilities for
each action. The Critic network mirrors the Actor network’s
structure, except in the final layer, where it outputs a single
feature through a fully connected layer with 128 neurons.
Fig. 9 illustrates the training process of the BSM as a
function of reward variation. Specifically, we conduct experi-
ments on a 4060ti with 12600kf cpu, 16G memory and 16G
video random access memory. The experiment took 12 hours
and 150000 iterations, and the optimal model was generated
around 70000 rounds. As the number of iterations increases,
the model’s reward value also rises. Between 60,000 and
80,000 epochs, the rewards begin to converge, suggesting
that an effective ABR algorithm has been achieved at this
stage. We then compared the performance of the obtained
ABR algorithm against several baseline algorithms, which are
described in detail below.
Baseline: The algorithms selected in this experiment are
representative algorithms in the field of video streaming ABR
at present.
• BBA [20]: A method based on ordinary buffer;
• BOLA [17]: Standard ABR solution to ABR problem by
Lyapunov function;
• RobustMPC(RMPC) [21]: The Model Predictive Control
(MPC) method was used to predict bitrates by combining
buffer occupancy and network throughput, but the error
between predicted and observed throughput was taken
into account by normalizing the throughput estimate to
the maximum error seen in the past five blocks;
• Pensieve [15]: Based on a regular DRL ABR scheme, we
use a pretrained model that uses 16 agents;
• QUETRA [38]: A DASH rate adaptive algorithm based
on queuing theory;
• Festive [19]: The rate-based algorithm, such as, uses
the harmonic average method to predict the bit Rate
according to the network throughput download of several
video blocks in the past, and limits the predicted bit rate
within a certain range;
• SAC-ABR [39]: The SAC-ABR algorithm is a reinforce-
ment learning algorithm based on the SAC algorithm;
• Genet [40]: Genet is built on curriculum learning, a new
training framework for learning better RL-based network
adaptation algorithms.
In the experiments, three key metrics are employed. The
video bitrate describes the relative quality of the video, with
higher bitrates indicating better video quality. Bitrate smooth-
ness characterizes the fluctuation range of video quality during
playback, where smaller fluctuations lead to superior user
experience. The time spent on stall reflects the frequency of
rebuffering during playback, and lower values are preferable.
As illustrated in Fig. 10(a), the Festive algorithm outper-
forms other algorithms by a significant margin in terms of
bitrate smoothness. However, its over-reliance on selecting
video chunks with high bitrates results in the longest buffer-
ing duration—an outcome clearly undesirable for users. The
buffering duration of the BPA algorithm is only half that of
Festive, while its bitrate smoothness is slightly inferior to
Festive. This implies that users can enjoy smoother video
playback while still obtaining a satisfactory bitrate. The Pen-
sieve algorithm performs marginally worse than BPA in both
bitrate smoothness and buffering duration. The SAC-ABR
algorithm achieves better bitrate smoothness than BPA but
is outperformed by BPA in buffering duration—a trend also
observed in the Genet algorithm. Although the BOLA and
QUETRA algorithms exhibit almost no buffering, their bitrate
smoothness is inferior to other algorithms. This means that
when using these two algorithms, the video resolution may
abruptly switch from 2K to 720p, a scenario that is obviously
unacceptable to users.
The percentage of time spent on stalls and the average video
bitrate by these algorithms are shown in Fig. 10(b). It can be
seen that the BPA algorithm has a good video bitrate with low
stall time. Although algorithms like BBA and RobustMPC are
able to have higher video bitrate, they spend almost 5 times
and 2 times more time on stalls than the BPA algorithm, which
is a bad experience for the user watching the video. QUETRA
algorithm has fewer stalls, but the difference in the average
video bitrate is also almost 0.1, which is also not what the
user wants to see. Both the SAC-ABR and Genet algorithms
are inferior to the BPA algorithm in terms of video quality
and buffering duration. Compared to the Pensieve algorithm,
BPA algorithm has fewer stalls and almost the same average
video bitrate.
Fig. 10(c) illustrates the average video bitrate and bitrate
smoothness of each algorithm. A good ABR algorithm must
have low bitrate smoothness and high video bitrate. It can be
seen that the BPA algorithm has a good average video bitrate
while having a low video smoothness compared to the other
algorithms in the graph. The Pensieve algorithm has about the
same video bitrate as the BPA algorithm but is a little bit
worse in terms of bitrate smoothness. The Festive algorithm
has the best bitrate smoothness, but it also has the lowest
average video bitrate The BBA algorithm has the highest video
bitrate, but also the worst bitrate smoothness, almost three
times that of the BPA algorithm. The SAC-ABR and Genet
algorithms outperform the BPA algorithm in bitrate smooth-
ness, indicating that these algorithms do not frequently switch
video quality. However, they are inferior to the BPA algorithm
in terms of video quality. This suggests that to mitigate the
penalty of quality switches, the two algorithms proactively
compromise on video quality, an outcome undesirable for
users. RobustMPC also has a high average video bitrate, but is
worse than our BPA algorithm in terms of bitrate smoothness.
```

```text
Although our algorithm loses a little bit of video quality, it
avoids switching the video bitrate frequently, which must be

It is crucial to verify if the BPA algorithm can achieve
a respectable QoE following the aforementioned comparative
experiments. We adopt Eq. (13) as the QoE metric and set the
α to 4.3.
Fig. 11 displays the cumulative distribution function (CDF)
of QoE values for several baseline ABR algorithms. The
results clearly show that the BPA algorithm outperforms all
other algorithms in the comparison. Specifically, BPA achieves
a QoE improvement of 31.9% over traditional heuristic algo-
rithms like BBA, 12.8% over BOLA, and 2% over Pensieve.
Compared with other deep reinforcement learning algorithms,
it achieves a 4% improvement over SAC-ABR and a 9.3%
improvement over Genet.
Finally, to illustrate the efficiency of the BPA algorithm.
To prevent the effects of different training algorithms, the
Pensieve algorithm uses the same DCPPO algorithm to train.
The same 16 agents are used as described in the original
Pensieve algorithm. In the experiment, it can be found that
more than 150,000 rounds of iterations are needed to obtain
the maximum cumulative reward [15]. However, for BPA algo-
rithm, it only needs 2 agents and 70,000 rounds of iterations to
find the maximum reward. Table III shows the rewards during
the training of the BPA algorithm and finds that, as expected in
```

```text
initial decline, our model gradually and adaptively increases
the entropy value. This change brings the advantage that our
model continues to explore the strategy space, avoiding the
phenomenon of entropy collapse.
V. CONCLUSION
In this paper, the BPA algorithm has proposed, an adaptive
bitrate selection method for video streaming based on network
bandwidth prediction. The BPA algorithm aims to optimize
video quality, minimize playback stalls, and enhance the user
experience by improving bandwidth prediction accuracy. BPA
achieves bitrate selection through two main modules: the BPM
and the BSM. BPM leverages a BiLSTM network to predict
bandwidth trends effectively, providing reliable forecast data
for BSM. The BSM module is built based on the Actor-Critic
framework and trained using the proposed end-to-end joint loss
function. It combines bandwidth prediction accuracy with QoE
objectives to make optimal bitrate selections. Experimental
results indicate that the BPA algorithm delivers smoother
playback and higher video quality compared to other ABR
algorithms. Furthermore, the BPA algorithm demonstrates
superior training efficiency, requiring fewer agents and iter-
ations to achieve optimal performance than comparable deep
reinforcement learning approaches.
```

```text
DETERMINATION OF PARAMETERS IN BPM
We carried out a verification experiment on the selection of
parameters t and n in BPM. Specifically, we use a small-scale
network traces dataset, randomly selecting 300 bandwidth data
to simulate the real network environment. The reason we opted
for a small-scale rather than a large-scale dataset is that the
former is more representative of actual network conditions.
In the experiment, the number of neurons was set at 128.
The parameter t took values from the set {1,2,3,4,5}, and the
parameter n from the set {1,2,3}. Through the experiment, we
discovered that when t > 5 and n > 3, the model prediction
would suffer from overfitting, rendering the predictive network
meaningless.
The experimental results are presented in Table A1, where
the MSE serves as the evaluation metric. It can be observed
that the prediction error of the model reaches its minimum
when t = 3 and n = 1. Additionally, it is noted that with t held
constant, as the prediction horizon n increases, the prediction
performance of the model gradually deteriorates.
VERIFICATION OF THE EFFECTIVENESS OF BPM
To verify the role played by the BPM in the network,
small-scale network traces dataset was utilized, and network
trajectories were randomly selected to simulate the network
environment. The parameter settings were t = 3, n = 1, and
the number of neurons was set to 128. The experimental results
are presented in the following figure.
The experimental results indicate that the BPM model
performs robustly even on smaller network traces datasets. As
illustrated in Fig. B1(a), BPM effectively captures the overall
trend of network fluctuations while also predicting bandwidth
values with high accuracy, an encouraging outcome. However,
it also can be found that BPM’s accuracy declines when
dealing with very small datasets or extremely low bandwidth
scenarios. For instance, in Fig. B1(b), while BPM captures
the general trend, the prediction error remains high for certain
peak data points. Additionally, we found that BPM’s predictive
accuracy improves under favorable network conditions.
ANALYSIS OF THE EFFECTIVENESS OF INDIVIDUAL
MODULES IN BPA
The BPA algorithm consists of two components: a Band-
width Prediction Model and a Bitrate Adaptation Decision
Model. To enable the joint optimization of these two models,
we have proposed a novel reward function and loss function.
To verify whether the improvement in overall performance
relies entirely on enhanced prediction accuracy rather than the
strategy structure itself, we conducted a series of experiments
to analyze the effectiveness of each module in BPA. These
experiments were performed on a small-scale network traces
dataset, and the results are presented in the table below.
Specifically, we compared the original BPA algorithm with
the prediction module against the algorithm with the prediction
model removed. Additionally, to demonstrate the effectiveness
of the structure, we included a comparison with the Pensieve
algorithm.
As shown in Table C1, it is evident that the BPA algorithm
with the prediction model achieves the optimal performance.
It outperforms the Pensieve algorithm in terms of average
video quality, features a shorter rebuffering duration, and
also excels in the video smoothness metric. When the pre-
diction model is removed from BPA, a slight performance
degradation is observed, yet it remains comparable to the
Pensieve algorithm—with a mere 0.01 difference in the QoE
metric. The primary reason for this phenomenon lies in the
fact that the BPA algorithm jointly optimizes the prediction
model and the decision model. During the training process, it
aims to improve prediction accuracy while optimizing bitrate
selection: the BPM outputs predicted values to enable the BSM
to perceive future bandwidth changes and adapt to the network
dynamically. Notably, even without the prediction model, the
standalone policy network of BPA still outperforms existing
traditional algorithms.

the Deep Q-Network (DQN) network as that of the Actor-
```

```text
The entropy value represents the uncertainty in the action
selection process. Initially, both AC and DQN start with
relatively high entropy, indicating exploration. However, the
AC structure shows a significantly quicker reduction in entropy
compared to DQN, suggesting that AC converges faster to an
optimal policy. The faster reduction in entropy indicates that
the AC structure is more effective in exploiting the learned
policy, thus ensuring more stability during training. The Fig.
D1(b) shows the cumulative reward achieved by the agent.
The AC structure consistently outperforms DQN in terms of
achieving higher reward values over time. The faster and
smoother curve in the AC plot indicates that it learns to
maximize rewards more efficiently than DQN, which lags
behind in achieving optimal performance. This demonstrates
that the AC structure not only converges faster but also leads
to better performance in terms of the task objective.
Given these observations, the AC structure was selected
due to its faster convergence and better reward maximization
compared to DQN. The ability to balance exploration and
exploitation effectively within the AC framework allows it
to outperform DQN, making it the preferred choice for the
current task.

THE DATASET USED IN EXPERIMENT
In the experiment, we used two network traces datasets
of different scalesand one video dataset as shown in Table
E1. The use of two different datasets serves to enhance
the generalization and stability of the model. Specifically:
Large-scale network traces datasets provide BPM with the
ability to learn broad patterns of bandwidth fluctuations,
helping to prevent overfitting that could arise from limited data
availability; Small-scale real-world network trajectory data is
used to validate the model’s applicability in actual network
environments and refine the bitrate selection strategy. This
combined approach ensures that the resulting BPA algorithm
adapts effectively to diverse network conditions.
DETAILED PARALLEL TRAINING ARCHITECTURE
The parallel training architecture illustrated in Fig. F1. In
the proposed framework, an agent refers to a complete training
instance that interacts with an independent Mahimahi network
environment and consists of two tightly coupled components:
a Bandwidth Prediction Module (BPM) and a Bitrate Selection
Module (BSM). The BPM is implemented using a BiLSTM
network to estimate future bandwidth ˆGt, while the BSM
adopts an Actor–Critic structure with DC-PPO to determine
the bitrate action at. Within each agent, bandwidth prediction
and bitrate selection are jointly optimized through the com-
bined loss function L = LDCPPO + λLt(G), enabling end-to-
end training.
```

```text
During training, two agents operate in parallel under differ-
ent network traces sampled from the dataset, independently
collecting interaction trajectories and computing gradients
based on their local experiences. A central parameter server
is employed to aggregate gradients from the parallel agents,
update the shared parameters—including the Actor network
parameters θ, Critic network parameters θv, and synchronize
the updated weights back to all agents. It is important to
emphasize that this central component functions solely as a
parameter synchronization mechanism rather than an addi-
tional decision-making agent. Compared with Pensieve, which
adopts 8-16 agents without an explicit bandwidth prediction
module, the proposed framework integrates a BiLSTM-based
predictor and performs joint end-to-end optimization with only
two synchronized agents, thereby maintaining a lightweight
yet stable training structure.
VALIDATION EXPERIMENTS FOR PARAMETER ω
To verify the value of the trade-off parameter ω in the
objective function, we conducted an experimental analysis.
Specifically, we used a small-scale network trajectory dataset
to simulate a real network environment, and models with
different ω values were iterated for the same number of rounds.
The experimental results are shown in the table G1.
As shown in Table G1, moderate values of ω (0.001–0.01)
achieve similar and optimal QoE performance. When ω = 0,
prediction accuracy does not influence policy learning, leading
to slightly higher rebuffering and lower QoE. As ω increases
beyond 0.05, the optimization increasingly prioritizes predic-
tion accuracy, resulting in more conservative bitrate selection
and gradual QoE degradation.
Overall, the results demonstrate that the proposed frame-
work is robust within a reasonable range of ω, and the selected
```
